newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore Airlines in on kangaroo route.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Airlines in on kangaroo route.

text.p: Singapore Airlines (SIA) has gained an important toehold in the lucrative Australia to Europe "kangeroo" route with its new four-airline alliance, boosting its position against other linkups, analysts said on Friday.
Its agreement to tie up with Australia's Ansett, Ansett International and Air New Zealand would not overtake its nearest rivals but would place it in a more competitive position.
"It's positive for SIA because it strengthens their network in the southwest Asia-Pacific region," said Nua We Boon, analyst with Fraser Securities.
SIA's alliance will pose a threat to the tie-up between Qantas and British Airways Plc on routes between Australia and Europe, they said.
It will also bolster its already extensive Asian operations as SIA will capture more passengers from Australia, filtering them into a market where it has an existing stronghold.
The alliance, described by the carriers as the largest in the Asia-Pacific, includes code-sharing, joint purchasing, joint marketing and cargo operations.
SIA, which flies to the major cities in Australia and New Zealand, will have access to new domestic destinations.
But all the airlines would benefit from the linkup in terms of being able to offer more comprehensive packages, the analysts said.
They said airline operations on such major passenger routes helped trim operating costs and offered freer access to previously shut domestic routes.
"All this just means that it will help per unit costs," said Lai Yeu Huan, an aviation analyst with J.M. Sassoon.
But he said the alliance was a defensive move to counteract the stranglehold on the kangeroo route by British Airways and Qantas, arguably entrenched in pole position.
In terms of the alliance enhancing earnings, Lai said it would not alter his modest outlook for SIA.
"I don't think the effect on earnings would be that great. The major impact would be on the cost side."
Lai, like others, felt British Airways and Qantas were the stronger team in terms of size and turnover.
"The outlook is very mixed, very dicey, and Qantas is going to fight tooth and nail," he said.
The gains for SIA, the strongest partner in the alliance, would have been clearer if the tie-up had included the carrier taking an equity share in one of the partners like Ansett.
"That would have signalled a greater commitment on both sides to mesh their services," Fraser's Nua said.
The alliance includes Ansett's fledgling Asian carrier, Ansett International as a separate partner. Ansett International is owned 49 percent by Ansett Holdings Ltd, the parent company.
Most analysts said SIA's taking a stake in Ansett was purely speculative, and not necessarity advantageous to SIA alone.
So far, the airlines' officials have refused to speculate about a possible future equity deal.
Ansett, jointly owned by News Corp Ltd and Air New Zealand, is the weakest financially of the partners.
"There could be some grounds because Ansett is not doing exactly very well. An equity stake by a foreign carrier could enhance its position," Nua said.
--Singapore newsroom (65 8703080)
